narrative: The model estimated a 95% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, this is a very high risk estimate, and because the law school treats that risk as too great, your application was rejected. The decision was driven most strongly by your LSAT score, which was 18 compared with an average of about 37 among accepted students; that gap pushed the prediction toward failure more than any other factor. The second strongest factor was your third-year class-rank decile of 1, far from the accepted average of about 5.8, and it also pushed toward failure. Your first-year class-rank decile of 1, again far from the accepted average of about 6, was the third most influential factor and likewise increased the predicted risk. Other information, such as your undergraduate GPA and family-income background, was not among the top drivers, though the overall profile still looked high-risk. To improve your chances, focus first on substantially raising your LSAT through structured preparation and a retake, and work with an admissions adviser on a plan to strengthen your academic record and class standing. Consider delaying reapplication until those changes are in place, and ask schools about conditional or provisional admission options.
